doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Race and covert control in the New York scene
summary: She describes covert business pressure over black and white groups, discussed with Billy Taylor.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: In New York is there any kind of racial scene connected with jazz that is uncomfortable or is there any issues about race these days in the music that you’ve been able to see?

Well if you were to look, as time has gone on, whether the music community has been polarized into black and white, I’ve felt that a lot, when it did exist, and when I saw it, it seemed like it was the musicians who are not in control of it, it felt like the music business community, the promoters, the club owners, were having more input into this, and the critics as well too I think, than I think the musicians. And that was a scary moment, a scary perception. That choices were being made about who musicians would play or not play with, based not on musical reasons, but something else. I remember there was a period, I remember talking with Billy Taylor about this in that interview, it probably wasn’t on the Charles Kuralt show, but I remember we had an interesting discussion about this. And he was very concerned about it too.
That there was control being exerted from—

Subtle. This is covert. I mean we’re not talking about overt stuff. It was covert pressure in terms of what was accepted in the club and what was considered the right thing and all black groups or all white, whatever it was. It was as if the musicians were not in control in deciding what they thought was best for their own musical development, who they should play with or who they shouldn’t. That was the real issue.
Who was trying to control it?

Oh it’s not a who, it’s not any particular person, it was prevalent in, you could see it in the way festivals and the way groups were lining up to play at certain clubs at certain places, and the way they were being recorded too. It’s not a finger pointing thing. It was — you could sense it in the consciousness of what was going on, and it had to do with also the kind of conservativism that had overtaken the music community as well too. I think it went hand in hand with what was going on with it in the country. In the class I spoke to here at the college we were talking about gender issues in music, and Dr. Woods brought up the fact that what was going on in the music community was reflecting what was going on in the society and the conservativism of the culture at the time as well. And I think there’s something very true in that.
